memoryText: Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Jeremiah 33:3 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse was spoken to a man in prison. Jeremiah was locked in the court of the guard while Jerusalem burned. He had nothing: no freedom, no city, and no apparent future. And God said, “Call to me.”

It is an invitation. The first thing God asks of someone in trouble is not to fix it but to call. Prayer is the simple act of speaking to God. No special words are required. The one who is in prison, who is at the end of his strength, can call.

“And I will answer you.” It is a promise. The word for answer includes the sense of responding to someone who has spoken. God is not deaf or distant. He hears and replies. Not every answer comes in the form or on the schedule we expect. But he answers. He had already answered Jeremiah’s earlier question by telling him to buy the field.

“And will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.” This is a surprise. God offers more than relief. He offers revelation. “Great and hidden” might also be translated “fortified, inaccessible.” There are things that human wisdom cannot reach. In Jeremiah’s case, God goes on to reveal the restoration of Israel, the righteous Branch, and the everlasting covenant. They are the most glorious promises of the book, and they came in prison.

Say this verse when you feel confined. God often does his greatest teaching in the narrowest places. Call to him. He will answer, and he will show you more than you thought to ask.
weekInReview: This week you finished the book of Jeremiah. You prayed Psalm 108, a song that begins with a steadfast heart and ends with trust in God because human help is vain. You read about the tragedy that followed the fall of Jerusalem: Gedaliah’s murder, the people’s request for God’s guidance that was already settled in their hearts, and their flight to Egypt in disobedience, where they took up idolatry again. You heard God’s quiet word to Baruch not to seek great things for himself. You read the oracles against Egypt, Moab, Edom, and above all Babylon, learning that no empire stands forever and even enemies have a future. And you read the closing chapter, which confirmed in history everything Jeremiah said and ended with Jehoiachin eating at the king’s table. The week taught that God’s word is reliable, that guidance requires willingness to obey, and that hope survives the fall.
reflectionQuestions: The people asked Jeremiah for God’s guidance but had already decided. Is there a decision in your life where you are asking God but have not truly surrendered the answer?
Baruch was told not to seek great things for himself. Where do you struggle with wanting recognition for your service?
Jeremiah’s longest prophecies ended with a king eating at a table in exile. Where might God be giving you a small sign of hope in a difficult season?
prayerPrompts: Call to God and ask him to tell you great and hidden things.
Thank him for his reliable word.
